1.pericope_label: In that day shall this song be sung in the land of Judah; we have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks. Open ye the gates, that the righteous nation which keepeth the truth may enter in
debates: Who is commanded to open the gates: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott hear a heavenly cry addressed to angels or heralds, Gill denies any such doorkeeper and applies it to the ministers of the gospel.
What the truth means: Clarke takes it for the gospel as against the shadowy rites it fulfils, Ellicott reads a plural covering every form of truthfulness in heart and life.
outliers: Clarke lays out the chapter as a hymn with changing speakers, and describes the prophet catching up the chorus as one instrument reverberates another tuned to the same key.
Clarke reports that the second noun means properly the ditch outside the wall, so that the pair are the wall and its outwork.
themes: A song written before the calamity it answers
The gates opened to a righteous nation

3.pericope_label: Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee. Trust ye in the Lord for ever: for in the Lord Jehovah is everlasting strength
debates: Whose firmness the third verse describes: Gill, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch read the steadfast mind of the believer, Calvin refers the firmness to God and makes the peace of the Church rest on his unchangeable purpose, arguing that otherwise the reason clause would be superfluous.

What the doubled divine name proves: Clarke connects the rock with the streams in the desert and identifies that rock as Christ, while Calvin rejects as ingenuity the inference of the divinity of Christ from the two names and takes them as magnifying God’s power.
outliers: Gill notes that the word perfect is absent from the Hebrew, which simply repeats peace; Ellicott says the italics of the English betray the interpolation.
Clarke reports the old versions differing on the last verb of the third verse, one giving they have trusted and two we have trusted.
themes: A purpose fixed in God rather than in us

5.pericope_label: For he bringeth down them that dwell on high; the lofty city, he layeth it low ... the way of the just is uprightness ... yea, in the way of thy judgments, O Lord, have we waited for thee
debates: What the seventh verse says of the just: Calvin denies that it praises their righteousness at all and makes the metaphor one of God applying a balance, while Gill offers three constructions and Ellicott would drop the weighing for a smoothing.
Whether the eighth verse is the church of the last days looking back or the prophet returning to his own present: Keil and Delitzsch argue for the first against commentators who hold the second.
outliers: Clarke notes three old versions reading the verb of waiting without its pronoun.
Ellicott suspects the vocative most upright should be taken adverbially.
themes: The proud city trodden by the poor

9.pericope_label: With my soul have I desired thee in the night ... let favour be shewed to the wicked, yet will he not learn righteousness ... Lord, when thy hand is lifted up, they will not see
debates: Whether the tenth verse contradicts the ninth: Calvin puts the objection against himself and answers that the profit of chastisement was never universal, the earlier statement meaning the elect.

Whether the clause about favour is a question or a concession: Calvin reports the reading that makes it Shall favour be shewed to the wicked, and prefers the concession, with Keil and Delitzsch taking it as a hypothetical clause marked only by emphasis.
outliers: Clarke reports forty-one manuscripts and five editions reading the verb of desire with its suffix, the omission of a letter having produced the third person elsewhere.
Ellicott borrows a poet’s line, that the mind is its own place and can make a hell of heaven itself.
themes: Kindness that teaches the wicked nothing
A hand lifted up and not seen

12.pericope_label: Lord, thou wilt ordain peace for us: for thou also hast wrought all our works in us ... other lords beside thee have had dominion over us ... they are dead, they shall not live ... thou hast increased the nation, O Lord
debates: How far the twelfth verse proves that God works all good in us: Henry takes it at full strength, Calvin grants the doctrine but denies that this verse establishes it and declines to press it in controversy.

Who the other lords are: Gill canvasses sin and Satan, the idols, the native governors and the foreign empires, and settles on persecuting tyrants; Ellicott takes the conquerors and possibly their gods; Calvin distinguishes rulers opposed to true worship from good kings who rule in God’s name.

What the fifteenth verse describes: Gill and Keil and Delitzsch read an increase of the people, Ellicott reports a Greek rendering making it a prayer for evils on the glorious, Wesley reads a removal into captivity where Ellicott reads a restoration of the old borders.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch warn that the fourteenth verse denies no resurrection in general, the prophet being acquainted with one; Calvin argues the same from the contrast with the nineteenth verse.
Ellicott records a Greek version making the shades physicians who shall not raise them up.
themes: All our works wrought for us
A nation increased and its borders moved out

16.pericope_label: Lord, in trouble have they visited thee, they poured out a prayer when thy chastening was upon them ... we have been with child, we have been in pain, we have as it were brought forth wind
debates: Whom the sixteenth verse describes: Calvin weighs hypocrites who flee to God only under constraint and decides for believers, since God instructs them by chastisement too.

What the last clause of the eighteenth verse means: Calvin knows a reading that makes the verb dwelling, so that the exiles shall not return, but prefers the ordinary sense and refers it to the wicked who do not fall; Ellicott keeps the birth image and renders that the inhabitants of the world were not brought to birth.
outliers: Clarke reports a professor identifying the figure with a specific disorder, a windy inflation of the womb that counterfeits pregnancy and ends in no birth, and notes an old version rendering the line that way.
Ellicott notes that the noun for prayer is used elsewhere of the whispered incantations of the heathen, and means here the low-toned prayers of the afflicted.
Clarke reports the Greek and two manuscripts putting the verb of seeking in the first person plural.

19.pericope_label: Thy dead men shall live, together with my dead body shall they arise. Awake and sing, ye that dwell in dust: for thy dew is as the dew of herbs, and the earth shall cast out the dead
debates: What resurrection is meant: Calvin rejects both the reading that confines it to the last judgment and the one that discharges it at the first coming, and takes in the whole reign of Christ; Ellicott reads it primarily of a national and spiritual rising; Clarke and Gill press it towards the rising of the body.
How the phrase about the prophet’s own body construes: Calvin lists three renderings and takes the words in immediate connection, so that the prophet counts himself among God’s dead men.
What the dew is: Clarke reads the dew of the dawn on three old versions, Ellicott allows the dew of herbs but reports that most render the dew of lights.
outliers: Clarke argues that the doctrine of the resurrection must already have been popular, since an image assumed for allegory must be commonly known or it will not answer its purpose.
Clarke reports all the ancient versions giving a plural, and two of them their dead bodies, a reading no manuscript confirms.
Ellicott notes that the verb for casting out the dead is another form of the one used just before of childbirth.
themes: Life promised to God’s dead men
The prophet numbering himself with them

20.pericope_label: Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment ... for, behold, the Lord cometh out of his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity
debates: Whether these verses belong to the song: Henry reports the view that they begin a new matter and introduce the following chapter, Keil and Delitzsch say the song is at an end, Gill allows both.
What the place is that God comes out of: Gill takes heaven, as a king leaving his throne, while Calvin prefers an allusion to the sanctuary and argues it expresses more.
What the indignation is: Calvin takes the affliction proceeding from God’s anger rather than the rage of enemies, without objecting to the other reading.
outliers: Henry recalls a banished bishop who told his grieving friends the trouble was only a small cloud that would soon blow over.
Ellicott reads a plural of intensity in the bloods of the earth.
themes: Chambers of distinction, defence and devotion
